**What this PR does / why we need it**:

@gnufied @bswartz fixed the PR. Please see my comments.

I still think it's worth calling the BLKGETSIZE64 ioctl on the block device after the rescan to validate the new size. Then if, for whatever reason, the new size isn't reflected, we can properly return failure and hope that a retry will solve the problem or that the error will get the notice of an administrator. If the rescan doesn't pick up the new size and the resize2fs call goes through we report success to the end user while not having actually changed anything.

@bswartz the problem that it is impossible to manage situations, when the block device geometry was successfully updated without the rescan. If we implement this logic, an error will be returned. We can try the `syscall.Statfs` call, which detects the filesystem size, not the block device size. This may be an option. Thoughts?

There is a similar request in https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-openstack/issues/777#issuecomment-535906933

I'm not suggested we check the siize before and after the scan and look for a change. I'm suggesting that we just check the size and only rescan if it's wrong, then check the size again and return an error if it's still wrong. We should have access to the size that the volume is supposed to be, and we can compare to that.

Am I missing something? Is there a case when it's not possible to get the size of a block device at all? I think it's worth also doing a statfs after the resizefs (to make sure that the resize command didn't break) but that would be in addition to checking the size of the block device. If the block device is the wrong size, then the resize command will be wasted.

> I'm not suggested we check the siize before and after the scan and look for a change. I'm suggesting that we just check the size and only rescan if it's wrong, then check the size again and return an error if it's still wrong. We should have access to the size that the volume is supposed to be, and we can compare to that.

Only CSI plugins support the `CapacityRange` and `CapacityBytes` info. But even with this info you cannot be 100% sure that you know the exact size of the volume, because in certain APIs you specify GiB, and I'm afraid that the resulting bytes size can be different due to possible overheads or wrong calculations. I wouldn't add the the rough volume size check logic...

UPD: not only CSI support the new size options, it is possible to pass them to the `GenericResizeFS`, then to the `Resize` func. But again, I'm not sure that all cloud providers provide volumes, that have the exact GiB size.

Well you only need to enforce the minimum size. Kubernetes always allows too-large volumes. I agree it can be tough to get the number exactly right though. For raw blocks, there are no overheads and it's just a matter of getting the math right (GB vs GiB), but for filesystem volumes the overheads are unpredictable.
@gnufied any updates on this PR?

> @bswartz let me know what do you think about the new change. CSI plugin developers have to consider this change and introduce additional code, e.g.:

This change looks good to be for kubelet. I'm not sure how CSI plugins are affected, unless they choose to import this code from k8s. Perhaps the cinder CSI plugin does that, but I'm not familiar with that plugin.

issue_context.title: resizefs package has to trigger a block device rescan before resizing the FS
issue_context.body:
**What happened**:

In some hypervisors, e.g. VMware, the new volume size is not pushed to the VM after the in-use block device extend, and you have to run the `echo 1 > /sys/block/sdb/device/rescan` manually and resize the FS manually.

**What you expected to happen**:

The `echo 1 > /sys/block/sdb/device/rescan` has to be executed before executing the resize2fs.

The `echo '- - -' > /sys/class/scsi_host/*/scan` is not enough for the vmware VM to get the new block device geometry. Nevertheless the `echo '- - -' > /sys/class/scsi_host/*/scan` is executed only during the volume attach.

**Environment**:
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: openstack
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`): coreos
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): 4.19.66-coreos

Regular Cinder plugin is affected, as well as the new CSI https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-openstack/pull/620

Some info https://unixutils.com/extending-space-existing-lundisk-extend-volumes-file-systems-linux/

review_comments: The comment is incorrect I think.
What is your suggestion? I used this comment as a source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/512eccac1f1d72d6d1cb304bc565c50d1f2e295e/pkg/volume/util/device_util_linux.go#L53
actually discard this comment. I see that we are resolving the symlink found in `/sys/block/sda/device/rescan` before returning it...

I do not have a system where I could test this right now but is new size immediately available after writing to `/sys/block/xxx/device/rescan` file? As the comment implies does this needs to poll for device geometry before calling ext/xfs resize utils? cc @bswartz

I recommend checking the block device size after rescaning and fail if the size hasn't been updated. If the update is synchronous, this is harmless. If the update is asynchronous and slow, then this will succeed during the next retry.
I looked at the kernel code and it appears that the rescan is in fact synchronous, but I still think that checking the size is good practice for defense against bugs elsewhere.

I don't think that the check has to be here. Let's assume that somewhen the device polling won't be necessary, in this case the device size won't be increased, and the function will fail the old size vs new size comparison check.

This should be kind of an opt-in. Not all volume types support rescanning and making this as core part of resizing workflow will break those plugins. For example on EBS:

```
# pwd
/sys/block/xvdbd/device
# ls
block  devtype  driver  modalias  nodename  power  subsystem  uevent
```

I am also wondering which in-tree plugins are targetted by this change? Is this change for CSI plugins that are vendoring k8s and using resize helper defined here?  If yes - we may want to do this as an optional flag to `Resize` function rather than making it a default.
It won't break, but show a log message. Though making this an option is a good idea. Do you have any suggestions on the option name?
I think passing a boolean flag called `rescanDevice` to `Resize` function makes sense. All of existing in-tree drivers will simply pass `false` but if any driver needs it they can opt-in.
